newsitem.title: USA: O.J. Simpson trial hears of bloody gloves, socks.
newsitem.headline: O.J. Simpson trial hears of bloody gloves, socks.

text.p: Supporting the defence claim that O.J. Simpson was framed, a forensic expert testified on Monday that blood could have been planted on his sock and that gloves similar to ones found at the murder scene and Simpson's estate did not shrink when soaked in blood.

The glove testimony in the civil trial on wrongful death charges was new since it had not been heard at last year's criminal trial, when defence attorney Johnnie Cochran told the jury if "they (the gloves) don't fit, you must acquit."

In the dramatic high-point of the criminal trial, Simpson tried on the bloody leather gloves for the jury and held up his hands to show that they apparently did not fit. He was subsequently found not guilty of murdering his ex-wife Nicole Brown Simpson and a friend, Ronald Goldman, on June 12, 1994.
The prosecution contended the gloves belonged to the ex-football star and were worn by the killer. They had shrunk after being soaked in blood, the prosecutors argued.

But at the civil trial, where Simpson is being sued for damages by relatives of the victims, forensic expert Herbert MacDonell said he carried out an experiment on gloves similar to the ones found at the murder scene and at Simpson's estate.

"I did not detect any measurable shrinkage in either glove," MacDonell told defence attorney Robert Baker. He explained he had soaked the two XL-size gloves with 2mm of his own blood and allowed it to soak into the leather gloves.

"I tried to duplicate the compression ... of people engaging in some kind of conflict," he said. "I spread it around to see how much blood I could force into the glove. I smeared it for 30 seconds and then it drained out into a funnel."
He then dried each glove, timing how long they took -- about four hours -- to become completely dry, and put them on a copying machine and measured them again to see if they had shrunk.

In further questioning by Baker, MacDonell, who is director of a forensic laboratory in New York state, also repeated his testimony from the criminal trial that the pattern of stains on a sock at Simpson's home indicated the blood may have been planted, as the defence contends.

Describing large photographs of a section of one of the bloody socks found in Simpson's bedroom, MacDonell said it would have been impossible for blood to have soaked through the way it did if someone was wearing it.

Asked by Baker if the pattern of blood stains could have resulted from someone putting blood on the sock, MacDonell replied: "Yes, like with a medicine dropper." He said he came to his conclusions by a process of elimination by microscopic examination of the stain, which DNA testing has concluded was Nicole Brown Simpson's blood.

"Blood did not drip, splash or splatter. It was transferred by touching or compressing or a lateral motion called swiping," he said. Also possible, he said, was that the pattern showed it could have been transferred "by a finger or a drop of blood added and teased around to create a stain."
"If there had been anything inside the sock, like a foot, when it was stained, then it would not have gone through and stained the other (inside) surface," he said.

Lawyers for the plaintiffs cross-examined MacDonell and got him to acknowledge he had not taken detailed notes about his findings on the sock stains. Also he could not say exactly how many specks had soaked through and many of them were so small they could not be definitively tested as blood.
The defence contends blood evidence on the socks could have been planted to implicate Simpson and that the whole forensic investigation of the murders was incompetently carried out.
